title: Beyond Net-Zero
excerpt: Being net-zero was never going to be enough for us. Here's how a spare cupboard, some old hardware, and a monthly beach walk became part of who we are.
content:
When I started The Break, I knew that the pillars of the company ethos would be community, environment, and creativity. I wanted an outlet to express my own creativity and to champion others; at the same time, I wanted to highlight the importance of nature and outdoors exposure in an ever-growing digital world. Recent years have seen a massive rise in smartphone use, from preteens all the way up to OAPs, and at The Break, we wanted to push people towards living more natural lives.

The final pillar was perhaps the most important one. **The environment**.

Of course, the materials we use are all organic and recycled, the shipping bags are compostable, the promotional stickers are vegan, and any card we use is biodegradable. But we didn't want to stop there — we wanted to go even further. Eventually, we moved our website servers away from large data centres and onto small IoT devices sitting in a cupboard in the flat, reusing old technology and cheap hardware to run power-efficient micro servers. (Eventually, we plan to hook up solar panels and run the entire thing using renewables.)

Ultimately, we decided that being net-zero was not enough; we wanted to be proactive. Starting on the 1st of January 2026, we announced that we'd be undertaking monthly litter picks. **Since then, we have achieved seven months' worth of picks and are excited to grow our group even more**.

Some days, we have plenty of people join us; other days, it's just myself and Archie, my co-founder. Either way, they are always an incredible way to start the day and, above all else, a good excuse to chat and catch up whilst doing something for the planet. If we're on the beach, we tend to end with a dip; if not, we often try to find a coffee place for afterwards.

If you want to get involved, or know a spot that could do with some attention, drop us a message. The more people, the more ground we can cover.

**The latest information will always be posted on the Events page** and across our social channels.

title: Not All Organic Cotton Is Created Equal
excerpt: "Organic" is one of the most overused words in fashion. We wanted to explain what it actually means, and why we only work with suppliers who can prove it.
content:
Organic cotton gets thrown around a lot as a buzzword, so we wanted to actually explain what it means, and why it's one of the non-negotiables at The Break.

At its simplest, organic cotton is grown without synthetic pesticides, fertilisers, or genetically modified seeds. That sounds like a small distinction, but it isn't. Conventional cotton is one of the most chemically intensive crops in the world; it uses a disproportionate share of global pesticides for the amount of farmland it occupies. Organic farming methods, by contrast, rely on crop rotation and natural processes to keep the soil healthy, which in turn uses less water and keeps the surrounding ecosystem, and the farmers working it, safer.

But "organic" on its own isn't a guarantee of anything unless it's backed up by proper certification. That's why we source our cotton through Stanley/Stella, who we chose specifically because they don't just claim to be sustainable, they prove it.

Stanley/Stella's cotton is GOTS certified (Global Organic Textile Standard), which is the industry's gold standard. It doesn't just look at the raw cotton, it tracks the entire supply chain, from the farm through to the finished garment, and includes both ecological and social criteria along the way. On top of that, their products carry OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certification, confirming there are no harmful chemicals in the finished fabric, and Global Recycled Standard (GRS) certification for the recycled materials they use elsewhere in their range. They're also a member of the Fair Wear Foundation, which focuses on the people behind the product, not just the cotton itself, and their materials are PETA-Approved Vegan.

We could have gone with a cheaper, uncertified "organic" cotton and taken the label at face value. We didn't want to do that. Part of being genuinely sustainable is being willing to have your supply chain checked, not just described.

None of this means organic cotton is a perfect fix. It still needs water, and it's not a magic solution to the fashion industry's environmental footprint. But it's a meaningfully better starting point than conventional cotton, and paired with the way we treat everything else, from packaging to postage, it's one more piece of doing this properly rather than just doing it quickly.

If you've got questions about where any of our materials come from, ask us. We'd rather explain it properly than let a label do the talking.

title: Thank You To Those Who Made It Count
excerpt: A year ago, we bet £4,000 of our own money on an idea between a few students. Eight months in, we'd paid it all back. Here's who made that happen.
content:
A year ago, The Break didn't exist. It was an idea between a few students who wanted to do something a bit different, and £4,000 of our own money, saved up from weekend jobs, that we decided to gamble on it.

Looking back, it feels like a genuinely mad thing to have done. We had no funding, no experience running a business, and honestly, no real idea if any of it would work. We just knew we cared about the three things we started with: **community**, **environment**, and **creativity**, and figured the rest we'd work out as we went.

Almost exactly eight months in, we paid off every penny of that £4,000 start-up cost. We still can't quite believe it. That money represents a genuine risk we took on ourselves, and the fact that it's paid off, entirely because people chose to support us, means more than we can really put into words.

So, this post is mostly just a thank you.

Thank you to everyone who came and found us at BU, AUB, and the local markets we've set up at over the year. Standing behind a stall is a strange, exposing way to run a business, you get instant, honest feedback, and every single conversation, every person who stopped to chat, browse, or just say something kind, has kept us going more than you probably realise.

Thank you to everyone who's followed along on social media. Building something in public is nerve-wracking, and having people actually engage with what we're doing, rather than just watching quietly, has made this feel like something bigger than just the two of us in a flat.

And thank you to everyone who's bought something from us. Every single purchase directly funded the next step, more materials, another market stall, another litter pick. None of this happens without that support.

We've also been lucky enough to work alongside some brilliant artists this year, Amy Ryalls, Youkki, and Kai Gheorgheasa, whose creativity has shaped a huge part of what The Break has become. Getting to collaborate with people who care about their craft as much as we care about ours has been one of the most rewarding parts of this whole year.

On top of that, we got to feature in two separate magazines as an upcoming company, **Bristol247** and **SEEGUL**, which still doesn't quite feel real. Being written about by people outside our own little bubble was a strange, brilliant reminder that other people are actually paying attention.

A year in, we're still small, still figuring a lot of it out, and still running servers out of a cupboard. But we've paid off our start-up costs, built something we're proud of, and met more genuinely lovely people than we ever expected to.

Here's to year two.

title: We Left the Cloud for a Cupboard
excerpt: Krystal ran on 100% renewable energy, and they're still doing good work. But even renewable-powered data centres use enormous amounts of electricity. So we started wondering: what if we didn't need one at all?
content:
When we started The Break, we hosted with Krystal, a UK-based provider that runs on 100% renewable energy. They were - and still are - doing good work. But after we'd been running for a while, we started thinking about the bigger picture. Data centres, even renewable-powered ones, use enormous amounts of electricity. A single large data centre can consume as much power as a small town. And even though they're increasingly running on renewables, they're still part of a complex infrastructure that's fundamentally about centralisation and scale.

That got us thinking: what if we didn't need a data centre at all?
So we moved our entire website onto a Raspberry Pi - a small, cheap, reused piece of hardware sitting in a cupboard in the flat, connected to our local network. For those unfamiliar, a Raspberry Pi is a tiny computer the size of a credit card that costs around thirty to fifty pounds. It consumes between two and four watts when serving web pages, which is hundreds of times less than what a traditional data centre uses. We weren't starting from scratch with brand new equipment; we were reusing old tech that might otherwise have been binned.

The shift from a professional hosting company to running our own servers on consumer hardware wasn't about being precious or trendy. It was about following the logic we'd already committed to: if you want to be genuinely sustainable, you have to look at every layer, not just the parts that sound good on a marketing page.
But we're not stopping there.

The cupboard setup works fine for now, but it's still drawing power from the grid. Our next phase is to move the Pi outside, give it an antenna for connectivity, and power the entire thing with a solar panel. Imagine a small weatherproof box, sitting outside, running your website, completely off-grid. No grid electricity, no data centre, no carbon footprint for the infrastructure itself. It's technically complex - you need battery backup for cloudy days, a charge controller to manage the panel, and a solid connection - but it's doable. And honestly, the fact that it's a challenge is part of why it appeals to us.

We know this sounds like something from a Silicon Valley fever dream, but the reality is stranger than the hype suggests. The infrastructure we take for granted — hosting, cloud storage, streaming services - has real environmental costs that get hidden behind marketing language like "green data centres" and "carbon neutral." Those things are better than their alternatives, but they're not zero impact. An actual, genuinely off-grid, solar-powered web server? That's closer to the real thing.

We'll share more about how this actually works once we've got it running. For now, the Raspberry Pi in the cupboard is a radical downgrade from the data centre - and that's the whole point.
